questions.q: Why is a paper's abstract described as 'never sufficient on its own' for understanding a claimed result?
options: It is a compressed sales pitch for the paper; the actual evidence lives in the results section and must be checked against the claim
Abstracts are not written by the paper's actual authors
Abstracts never contain any true information
Journals require abstracts to be misleading by policy
questions.explain: The lesson calls the abstract a compressed sales pitch useful for deciding whether to read further, but says the actual claim must be checked against what the results section's data actually shows.

questions.q: Which section does the lesson say is most commonly skipped, causing readers to miss a paper's real limitations?
options: The appendix/supplementary material
The abstract
The title
The author list
questions.explain: The lesson states that skipping the appendix, which often contains exact hardware specs, gate counts, or raw data, is the single most common way readers miss a paper's real limitations.

questions.q: A paper claims a 'quantum speedup' but reports a single run with no error bars on known-noisy hardware, and provides no classical baseline timing. Per the lesson's red flags, what should this prompt?
options: Skepticism about whether the claim, as stated in the abstract, is actually supported by what was measured
Immediate acceptance, since any speedup claim on real hardware is automatically credible
The conclusion that the paper is fraudulent and should be reported
No concern, since error bars are irrelevant for quantum hardware
questions.explain: The lesson lists exactly these two signs -- no classical baseline and a single run with no error bars on noisy hardware -- as red flags that the claim may be broader than what the data actually supports, which calls for skepticism, not either accusation of fraud or automatic acceptance.

questions.q: In the repeatable reading pass, why does the lesson recommend reading the results section's figures/tables BEFORE reading the methods section in detail?
options: Knowing the actual result first makes the methodology's purpose concrete instead of abstract when you then read it
Methods sections are always wrong and should be skipped entirely
Results sections are always shorter and faster to read
Journals require results to be read first by convention
questions.explain: The lesson explains this ordering specifically: reading methods after you already know the result makes the methodology's purpose concrete, rather than reading an abstract procedure with no context for why it matters.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a credibility signal worth checking before investing time in a paper?
options: Whether the hardware or simulator used is named specifically, with version/calibration details
Whether the paper has a colorful cover image
Whether the paper is longer than 20 pages
Whether the authors have a large social media following
questions.explain: The lesson lists naming the exact hardware/simulator with version numbers, citation patterns, reported error bars, and code/data availability as credibility signals -- not page count or social media presence.
